title: When the Orchard Sings
premise: In 1898, on a colonial pearling coast, Tamsin Fairweather has spent her life as company property—indentured, uncounted, and careful to be seen as nothing. When a census taker's stray question reveals that the trading company has been falsifying indenture rolls to erase debts owed to divers' families, Tamsin finds herself holding the original ledger that proves it. To get it past three checkpoints and into the hands of a visiting magistrate before the fleet sails, she must ally with the one person she distrusts most: the census taker's son, who owes his own quiet debt to the company. She delivers the ledger at cost—the orchard her mother planted is burned in reprisal—but its testimony frees the indentured families, and Tamsin, finally counted, chooses to stay and rebuild rather than flee.
about_author: Jonah Yarrow is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing colonial shipping records before turning to fiction. They write about people history filed under 'miscellaneous,' and live within sight of water they still don't entirely trust.

chapters.title: What the Water Keeps
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Opening on the pearling fleet's return, we learn how she measures the world in carryable things: her mother's pearl knife, a dried orange from the orchard she isn't allowed to visit. Emotional beat: competent loneliness—she is useful to the company and invisible to everyone else.

chapters.title: The Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A census taker named Aldous Renner arrives to count the compound, and his casual question about her mother's name doesn't match anything in the company's roll. Tamsin realizes the ledger he carries contradicts the one in the factor's office. Emotional beat: the vertigo of discovering your whole life was misfiled on purpose.

chapters.title: Ledger of Small Debts
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, with a flashback to her mother. She breaks into the factor's office and finds the true roll: wages withheld, deaths unrecorded, families erased. She takes the original ledger, telling herself it's theft. Emotional beat: fear braided with a fierce, unfamiliar sense of rightness.

chapters.title: The Son Who Counts
chapters.summary: Alternating POV begins: Elias Renner, the census taker's son and a junior clerk for the company, notices the ledger missing and suspects Tamsin. Instead of reporting her, he covers for her—because his father's own name appears in the erased column. Emotional beat: reluctant complicity; two liars recognizing each other.

chapters.title: Three Checkpoints
chapters.summary: Dual POV. The plan forms: the magistrate arrives in nine days at the harbor, behind three checkpoints—the gatehouse, the customs shed, the company wharf. Each requires papers neither of them can fully forge. Emotional beat: rising tension as the scale of the company's reach becomes clear.

chapters.title: The Orchard Sings
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She visits her mother's abandoned orchard outside the walls to hide the ledger between visits, and finds other indentured families secretly tending it—a community she never knew existed because she never let herself be seen. Emotional beat: belonging offered, and the terror of accepting it.

chapters.title: What Loyalty Costs
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. The factor, Mr. Calloway, tests Elias's loyalty by making him sign the falsified new roll himself. Elias signs—and immediately regrets it, realizing the company now owns a piece of his handwriting too. Emotional beat: shame, and the understanding that loyalty to a lie is just another form of indenture.

chapters.title: The Gatehouse Burn
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A fire at the gatehouse forces the first checkpoint closed but brings soldiers and suspicion down on the compound; Calloway announces the orchard will be cleared for 'quarantine.' Tamsin must move the ledger early or lose everything. Emotional beat: desperation sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Past the Wharf
chapters.summary: Climax, dual POV. Tamsin walks the ledger through the final checkpoint sewn inside her diving jacket while Elias creates a diversion at the customs shed—knowing it will end his career. She reaches the magistrate as the fleet prepares to sail, and Calloway arrives to denounce her as a thief. Emotional beat: breathless courage; the moment of being seen and refusing to flinch.

chapters.title: Counted
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, epilogue-like. The magistrate voids the false rolls; Calloway is recalled under investigation. The orchard is scorched but the roots hold, and the families return to tend it. Tamsin gives her full name—for the first time—to the new census. Emotional beat: quiet, hard-won resolution; staying is itself an act of inheritance.
